planting.note: Wire or glue onto bark, cactus skeletons, or driftwood rather than potting in soil; this dry-forest species colors up best with strong light.

directions: In its native dry forests of southern Mexico and El Salvador, this spiky, triangular-leaved rosette grows perched on cacti and acacia trees rather than in soil, so mount it on bark or a similar open support with the base left unobstructed. Give it the brightest light you can manage short of scorching sun, since the foliage shifts dramatically from olive green toward a rich gold and brick-red tone under strong light, a color change that stays muted in deep shade. Soak or thoroughly mist once a week, then set it somewhere with brisk airflow so the tightly overlapping leaf bases dry out within a few hours. Avoid letting water sit in the central cup for extended periods, since this species is adapted to quick wet-dry cycles rather than constant moisture.

planting.note: Mount on bark or grow in an open, fast-draining basket; the popular giant cultivated form needs more room than the smaller wild-type rosettes.

directions: Native across Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, this species forms an open rosette of semi-stiff, silvery-gray leaves and sends up a distinctive pyramid-shaped, semi-pendent flower spike with peach-orange bracts and white petals. A much larger cultivated 'giant form' has circulated among growers since the 1980s and is noticeably bigger than typical wild specimens, so size expectations vary by source plant. Water more generously than desert-type tillandsias, soaking thoroughly once or twice a week, since it tolerates a bit more consistent humidity than silver-leaved arid species. Provide bright, filtered light and ensure the rosette drains and dries fully after watering to prevent basal rot.

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted; this slow-growing, cold-sensitive species flowers only once per rosette, so protect it well to let it reach that stage.

directions: Found growing as an epiphyte across Trinidad, Tobago, Venezuela, Colombia, and Brazil, this species forms a soft, fountain-like cascade of fine, silvery-sage leaves covered in fuzzy trichomes. Each rosette flowers only once in its life, producing pink-to-purple blooms, and typically leaves behind just two or three offsets that stay tightly fused to the base rather than separating easily. Protect it from both hot direct sun and cold drafts, since it is more cold-sensitive than many air plants, and soak it for about twenty minutes every seven to ten days with light misting in between in dry air. Ensure quick, complete drying afterward, since the dense trichome coat can trap moisture against the leaf surface.

planting.note: Mount on bark or a lithophyte-style rock setup; this wet-forest species wants more regular moisture than desert-adapted tillandsias.

directions: Ranging from Suriname south to Misiones province in Argentina, this species grows as an epiphyte or lithophyte in humid forest, forming a compact rosette that sends up an upright spike of vivid rose-pink bracts. Small blue-violet flowers emerge from the bracts in paired clusters, giving rise to the common name, with bloom typically concentrated in the cooler part of the year. Because it hails from consistently wet forest rather than arid scrub, water it more generously than silver-leaved desert tillandsias, soaking it two to three times a week. Provide bright, indirect light and good airflow around the leaf bases to prevent the frequent watering this species favors from causing rot.

planting.note: Mount on bark or wood in a bright spot with strong airflow; this species tolerates more direct sun than most soft-leaved air plants once established.

directions: Native from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, this canopy epiphyte produces a flattened inflorescence that lives up to its name by combining red bracts, yellow petals, and blue-violet petal tips all in one bloom. Give it bright light, including some direct morning sun once mature, since it handles more exposure than many of the softer, trichome-heavy air plants from drier habitats. Soak thoroughly once a week or mist daily in humid conditions, then shake off excess water and let it dry within a few hours in a well-ventilated spot. Keep it mounted rather than potted, since standing water at the leaf bases is the most common cause of failure in cultivation.

planting.note: Mount on bark with strong airflow; this thick-leaved, higher-elevation species wants drier conditions than most rainforest tillandsias and is still uncommon in cultivation.

directions: Found at higher elevations across Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, this species forms a dense rosette of thick, stiff, gray-green leaves and sends up a tall, feathery spike of large white flowers prized for an intense gardenia- or citrus-like fragrance, among the strongest of any tillandsia grown. Because its native habitat is drier and cooler than the lowland rainforest many air plants come from, let it dry out more fully between waterings and avoid the frequent misting that soft-leaved species need. Provide strong, indirect light and excellent air movement around the thick leaf bases, which are more prone to rot if kept damp too long. It remains relatively uncommon in specialty collections, so expect it to take several years to reach flowering size.
